title: Resort Brand Positioning: Decide Who Your Resort Is For
excerpt: How to position a resort in India: choose your main guest, find the reason they should pick you, write a positioning statement and keep it consistent across OTAs, site and social.
description: Resort brand positioning: choose your guest, define why they pick you, write a positioning statement and keep it consistent on OTAs, site and social.
html:
Resort brand positioning is a clear, written decision about who your resort is for, what occasion it serves best, and the one reason a guest should choose it over similar properties nearby. Once decided, it should show up identically in your OTA listings, website, Google profile and social media, so guests recognise the same promise everywhere.

Why most resorts end up sounding the same

Read ten resort listings in Coorg, Wayanad or Lonavala and you will see the same words: "nestled in nature", "luxury", "perfect for families, couples and corporates". When a property tries to appeal to everyone, it gives no one a reason to pick it. Guests then compare on price, which is the hardest position for a small property to win.

Positioning is not a logo or a tagline. It is a choice. The choice is uncomfortable because it means saying, in effect, "we are not the best place for some guests". But it makes every other marketing decision easier, from which photos to lead with to which ads to run.

Choose who the resort is for

Start with the guests you already serve well, not the ones you wish you had. Look at last year's bookings and reviews and ask which group booked most, stayed longest, complained least and returned.

Common primary audiences for Indian resorts:

  • Families with young children: need safe pools, kid-friendly food, activities, larger rooms or interconnected rooms.
  • Couples: privacy, views, good food, quiet, special-occasion touches.
  • Corporate offsites: meeting space, reliable Wi-Fi and power, group activities, easy access from a metro, GST invoicing.
  • Weddings and family functions: lawns or halls, enough rooms for guests, catering, décor partners, permissions.
  • Friends' groups: villas or dorm-style rooms, outdoor activities, flexible meal timings.
  • Long-stay and remote workers: desks, Wi-Fi, laundry, monthly rates.

Pick one primary audience and at most one secondary. A Rishikesh riverside property might be for yoga and wellness travellers first, with small corporate retreats second. That does not mean turning other guests away; it means your marketing leads with one group.

Find the reason to choose you

For your chosen audience, list what you offer that comparable properties within a couple of hours do not. Be concrete. "Great views" is not a reason; "every cottage faces the Kabini backwaters" is.

Useful questions:

  • What do guests mention in reviews without being asked?
  • What would be hard for a competitor to copy: location, land, a heritage building, a specific cook, an owner who hosts?
  • What occasion do you serve unusually well, such as a first family holiday with a toddler, or a 30-person offsite?
  • What can a guest do here that they cannot do at the resort down the road?

Most properties end up with two or three real differences. Pick the one that matters most to your primary audience.

Write a positioning statement

A positioning statement is an internal sentence, not an advertisement. It keeps staff, agencies and photographers aligned. A workable format:

For [primary audience] looking for [occasion or need], [resort name] is the [category] in [location] that [main reason to choose], because [proof].

An example, illustrative only: "For Bengaluru families with children under ten looking for a weekend away, this is the resort in Coorg where kids have a supervised activity programme every day, because we run a dedicated kids' club with trained staff and a fenced play area."

Test it with three questions. Is it true today, not after a future renovation? Would a guest care? Could a nearby competitor say exactly the same thing? If the answer to the last one is yes, keep working.

Turn positioning into choices

Once written, positioning should change real decisions. A short worksheet helps.

AreaQuestionExample for a family-first resort
Lead photoWhat image shows the main reason to choose you?Children at the pool or in the play area, not an empty room
Listing headlineDoes the first line name your audience or occasion?"Family resort in Coorg with daily kids' activities"
Room namesDo they help the audience choose?"Family Cottage (2 adults + 2 kids)" instead of "Deluxe Premium"
PackagesDo they fit the occasion?School holiday package with meals and activities
PoliciesAre the ones this audience cares about clear?Child age and extra bed rules on every listing
Social contentDo most posts speak to this audience?Kids' club moments, family meals, parent-friendly tips

Keep it consistent across OTAs, website and social

A guest might see your Instagram Reel, look you up on MakeMyTrip, then check your website and Google listing. If each one describes a different resort, trust drops. Consistency is one of the cheapest improvements you can make.

A consistency checklist

  • The same resort name, spelling and location description everywhere.
  • The same first sentence or two of description across OTAs, Google and your site.
  • The same room names and inclusions on every channel.
  • The same lead photo set, in the same order.
  • The same main reason to choose you in your Instagram bio and website header.
  • The same policies for children, pets, cancellations and meals.

Review all of these together once a quarter. Staff changes and quick edits on one OTA extranet cause drift over time.

Positioning also guides your visual assets; the shot lists in our post on resort photography and video should follow from it. If your property makes environmental claims as part of its identity, read eco branding without greenwashing before writing them. For a wider view of how this fits with every channel, see the hospitality page and our content marketing approach.

Frequently asked questions

Will positioning for one audience lose me other guests?

Usually not. Positioning decides who your marketing leads with, not who you accept. A family-first resort can still host couples and offsites; it simply stops describing itself in vague terms that appeal to no one. In practice, a clear focus tends to make the resort easier to remember and recommend, including for guests outside the main audience.

How is brand positioning different from a tagline?

Positioning is the decision about who you serve and why they should choose you. A tagline is one short public expression of that decision, and many good resorts do not have one. Write the positioning statement first, as an internal reference. If a tagline comes out of it naturally, use it; if not, a clear listing headline does the same job.

Can a resort have different positioning for weekdays and weekends?

It can have different offers, but the core identity should stay the same. A Lonavala resort might target families at weekends and corporate offsites on weekdays, with separate packages and landing pages for each. The description, photos and reason to choose the property should still feel like one place, so guests are not confused when they compare listings.

How often should resort positioning change?

Rarely. Revisit it when something significant changes, such as a major renovation, a new wing aimed at a different guest, or a clear shift in who books. Otherwise, consistency over several years builds recognition. Review the execution, including photos, descriptions and listings, every quarter, but keep the underlying positioning stable unless the evidence clearly says otherwise.

Where to start

Pull last year's bookings and reviews and identify the guest group you serve best. Write a one-sentence positioning statement using the format above and test it against the nearest three competitors. Then rewrite the first two lines of your Google and main OTA descriptions so they say the same thing.
